rationale: B wins because it catches the autonomy story A keeps trying to overstate. B's "The Enterprise AI Agent That Insists Humans Stay in the Loop" turns the approval requirement into a real angle, while A's "Ramp's new AI agent emails vendors" commits the sin its proof section later has to walk back. B still has one deck-slide reach in "$80 Billion Payments Network," but it gives the founder slightly cleaner press lanes with fewer faceplants.
gaps_in_A: "Ramp's new AI agent emails vendors" overstates the facts; the update says the agent drafts cancellation or renegotiation emails that finance approves, not that the agent sends them.

"Spend visibility alone didn't save these 200 companies" rests on "presumably" existing Ramp customers with prior spend visibility. That premise is not in the update, and the headline states it as fact.

"Software vendors now face a new kind of renewal call: a negotiation with an AI agent" sells a negotiation the facts do not prove. At most, vendors receive a finance-approved email drafted by software.
"An AI agent is now doing part of the procurement analyst's job" is plausible, but it needs the labor-market proof the set admits is not supplied; otherwise it drifts into workforce-impact theater.
gaps_in_B: "Ramp Turns Its $80 Billion Payments Network Into a Procurement Intelligence Engine" is a strategic inference, not a supplied fact. The update does not prove payment-level data powers the agent or gives Ramp an edge over standalone tools.
"200 real customers" changes "200-company beta" into customers. Maybe true, but not given; do not upgrade beta participants into customers without proof.
"SaaS vendors profit structurally from auto-renewals and shelfware" is plausible, but external to the update. It needs sourcing or softer framing before it becomes the spine of an angle.

The next step jumps to "journalist-fit-check." Before matching reporters, the founder still needs to pick the lead angle and secure the missing proof, especially methodology and a named beta customer.
